lead: A sensor turns a physical stimulus into a measurable electrical change. The trick is not electrical: it is a known physical law. A force bends a beam and changes strain gauge resistance; two dissimilar metals joined at two junctions, with the junctions at different temperatures, make a small emf; light creates charge carriers. The principles group by energy domain — mechanical, thermal, electrical, magnetic, radiant, chemical — and name the measurand, the intermediate variable and the electrical output. The same law often serves two measurands; the packaging, not the equation, decides what the sensor measures. That is how a phone knows orientation and a car knows tyre pressure.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for active and passive vocabulary, and basic electricity and magnetism — charge, field, potential, Ohm's law and Faraday's law.

blocks.text: Every sensing path has five stages: stimulus → sensing element → physical law → parameter change → electrical output. The law is the middle: it converts a non-electrical quantity into ΔR, ΔC, ΔL or Δemf. A resistance change needs a bridge or divider; a capacitance change needs an AC bridge or charge amplifier; an emf can go straight to a high-impedance amplifier. A passive sensor changes R, C or L and needs a supply; an active sensor makes its own emf (see Chapter 1.1).

Electrical quantities are the language. Charge Q is in coulombs (C). Note that C is also the usual symbol for capacitance, in farads; here the coulomb and the farad are different quantities. Electric field E = V/d is in volts per metre (V/m), with V the potential difference in volts and d the plate separation in metres. Potential energy per charge is V. For a capacitor, Q = CV, so C = Q/V, in farads (F). A parallel-plate capacitor has C = εA/d, where A is plate area in m², ε = ε₀εᵣ is permittivity in F/m, ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m, and εᵣ is relative permittivity. These equations are why a capacitive sensor needs a changing gap, area or dielectric.

Resistance is R = ρL/A. R is in Ω; ρ is resistivity in Ω·m; L is length in m; A is cross-section in m². Stretching a wire increases L and decreases A, so R rises; in a semiconductor the strain also changes ρ itself, which is the piezoresistive effect. Both are summed in the strain-gauge equation ΔR/R = GF·ε, where GF is the gauge factor (dimensionless), ε is strain (m/m) and ΔR is the change in resistance. It works under a steady load. A metal gauge has GF near 2, mostly from the change of shape; a semiconductor gauge reaches 50 to 200 but is far more temperature-sensitive. A load cell weighs a truck this way; construction and bridges come with the resistive transducers and strain gauges.

Piezoelectricity is different. A stress on quartz or PZT displaces charge: q = d·F, where q is charge in coulombs, d is the charge coefficient in C/N, and F is force in newtons. It gives a voltage across the crystal capacitance. It cannot hold a steady reading because the charge leaks away, so it suits vibration, impact and ultrasonic pulses. Piezoelectric transducers are treated with the piezoelectric and Hall-effect sensors.

Thermal law: the Seebeck effect. Two different metals joined at two points with a temperature difference ΔT produce an emf e = S·ΔT, where S is the Seebeck coefficient in V/K. The measurand is temperature difference; the output is a small dc voltage, often µV to mV. Cold-junction compensation is needed before you can read absolute temperature; the thermocouple laws come with the thermocouples, among the resistive transducers.

A coil has L ≈ N²µA/l, where L is inductance in henries (H), N is turns, µ is core permeability in H/m, A is core area in m², and l is magnetic path length in m. Faraday’s law gives e = −N·dΦ/dt, where e is induced emf in volts, Φ is the magnetic flux through one turn in webers (Wb), and t is time in seconds; the minus sign is Lenz’s law. A moving core changes reluctance and therefore L. A magnetostrictive material changes permeability under stress, so a coil around it reads force. Hall effect: VH = RH·I·B/t, where VH is the Hall voltage in volts, RH is the Hall coefficient in m³/C, I is current in amperes, B is flux density in tesla, and t is sheet thickness in metres. It senses a magnetic field or, with a fixed magnet, position.

Radiant laws: the photovoltaic effect gives an emf when light creates electron–hole pairs across a junction; the photoconductive effect lowers resistance when photons add carriers. The measurand is irradiance or wavelength; the intermediate is carrier generation; the output is emf or ΔR. A photodiode in a light meter is one use. Photodiodes and phototransistors have their own chapter with the optical sensors.

Chemical: a hygroscopic layer absorbs water, changing its resistance or capacitance. The measurand is relative humidity; the intermediate is water uptake; the output is ΔR or ΔC. A capacitor can sense displacement or humidity: the equation C = εA/d is the same, but one package lets pressure change d, and another lets humidity change εᵣ. Packaging decides. Humidity sensors come with the chemical sensors.
The same handful of laws runs most medical sensors:

examples.question: A capacitive pressure sensor has two plates of area A = 25 mm² separated by d = 0.10 mm of air (εᵣ ≈ 1, ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m). Pressure pushes the gap down by 0.01 mm. Find C before and after, the change in pF, the percentage change, and the small-signal sensitivity |dC/dd| at the start in pF/µm.
steps: Convert: A = 25 mm² = 25×10⁻⁶ m². Initial gap d₁ = 0.10 mm = 1.0×10⁻⁴ m. New gap d₂ = 0.10 − 0.01 = 0.09 mm = 9.0×10⁻⁵ m. Air gives ε = ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m.

Small-signal sensitivity at the start: |dC/dd| = ε₀A/d₁² = C₁/d₁ = 2.2135×10⁻¹² / 1.0×10⁻⁴ = 2.2135×10⁻⁸ F/m. Since 1 pF/µm = 1×10⁻⁶ F/m, this is 0.0221 pF/µm ≈ 0.022 pF/µm. The sign is negative physically: C rises as d falls.

traps: Do not confuse piezoresistive with piezoelectric. Piezoresistive changes resistance under strain and works for steady loads; piezoelectric makes charge under stress and cannot hold a steady reading without charge leakage.

The capacitance formula is non-linear in d. A 10 % reduction in gap (d falls to 0.9 d) raises C by about 11 % (1/0.9 = 1.111), not 10 %; a 10 % increase in gap lowers C by about 9.1 %. The relation is non-linear and not symmetric.
A Seebeck emf depends on the temperature difference, not the absolute temperature. A thermocouple still needs a cold junction before it reports absolute temperature.
In V<sub>H</sub> = R<sub>H</sub>·I·B/t, the thickness t is in the denominator. Doubling the sheet thickness halves the Hall voltage for the same current and field.
A photovoltaic cell gives an emf; a photoconductive cell changes resistance and needs a bias supply. They are not interchangeable circuits.

quiz.q: State the piezoresistive relation and define GF and ε.
quiz.a: ΔR/R = GF·ε. GF is the gauge factor, dimensionless (about 2 for metal gauges). ε is strain, ΔL/L, dimensionless. ΔR/R is the fractional change in resistance.

quiz.q: Why can a piezoresistive strain gauge hold a steady reading under a constant force, while a piezoelectric sensor cannot?
quiz.a: A piezoresistive gauge changes resistance as long as the strain exists, so a DC bridge can read it. A piezoelectric crystal produces charge q = d·F, but that charge leaks through the crystal and the circuit, so the output decays. It needs a changing force.

quiz.q: A parallel-plate capacitive sensor has A = 100 mm² and d = 0.20 mm of air. Find C. The gap then falls to 0.18 mm. Find the new C and the percentage change.
The same parallel-plate capacitor can be sold as a displacement sensor or a humidity sensor. What changes in each package, and why is the equation not enough to tell them apart?
quiz.a: Both use C = εA/d. In the displacement package, the measurand moves the plates and changes d. In the humidity package, a hygroscopic dielectric absorbs water and changes εᵣ. The equation is identical; the packaging and the exposed material decide which variable the outside world can change.

quiz.q: A thermocouple has Seebeck coefficient S = 40 µV/°C and sees a temperature difference ΔT = 25 °C. Find the emf.
A Hall sensor follows V<sub>H</sub> = R<sub>H</sub>·I·B/t. What happens to V<sub>H</sub> if the active sheet is made thinner, with the same current and field?
quiz.a: V<sub>H</sub> rises in inverse proportion to t: halving t doubles V<sub>H</sub> for the same I and B. The limits are the higher resistance, self-heating and the strength of the thin sheet.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same laws reappear in MEMS: a piezoresistive diaphragm in a phone barometer, a thermopile in an infrared forehead thermometer, a capacitive humidity layer in a weather station. Search next for MEMS piezoresistive pressure sensor and thin-film thermopile.
